title: Kung Pao Chicken
blurb: The takeaway classic, minus the gloop. Peanuts, dried chilli and a sharp-sweet sauce that thickens in the last thirty seconds.

ingredients.prep: cut into 2 cm lengths, white and green kept apart

steps: Toss the chicken with 1 tsp cornflour and 1 tbsp of the soy sauce. Leave it while you do everything else — this is velveting, and it is why restaurant chicken is never dry.
Start the rice: rinse 150 g jasmine rice until the water runs clear, add 190 ml water, lid on, boil then 12 minutes on the lowest heat. Don't lift the lid.
Mix the sauce in a cup: the remaining 2 tbsp soy, the sherry, vinegar, sugar and the last 1 tsp cornflour. Stir until no lumps.
Get a large frying pan or wok very hot with the oil. Add the chicken in one layer and leave it alone for 2 minutes so it browns, then stir-fry 2 minutes more until just cooked. Tip it onto a plate.
Same pan, heat down to medium. Add the chilli flakes, Sichuan pepper if using, garlic, ginger and the white parts of the spring onion. Stir for 30 seconds — you want fragrant, not brown.
Chicken back in, pour the sauce down the side of the pan. It will thicken and go glossy in about 45 seconds. Take it off the heat the moment it coats the chicken.
Stir through the peanuts and the green spring onion tops. Serve on the rice.
tips: Dried whole chillies are more authentic than flakes — if your store has them, use 6 snipped in half and fry them first in the oil until they darken.
No sherry? A tablespoon of stock plus a few drops of vinegar keeps the sauce balanced.

title: Nasi Goreng
blurb: The Netherlands' unofficial national dish. Every ingredient is a Dutch supermarket staple, and cold leftover rice makes it better than fresh.
steps: If you don't have cold rice, cook 150 g jasmine rice now and spread it on a plate in the fridge for 20 minutes. Warm rice turns to porridge in the pan.
Fry the eggs in a little oil, sunny side up with crisp edges. Set aside — they go on top at the end.
Heat the oil in your largest pan. Onion and carrot first, 4 minutes until softening.
Add the chicken and fry 4 minutes until it colours. Then the garlic, coriander, cumin, laos and sambal — 1 minute, stirring, until the kitchen smells like an Indonesian toko.
Cabbage in, 2 minutes, then the cold rice. Break up the lumps with the back of your spoon and let it fry undisturbed for a minute at a time so it catches slightly.
Pour over the ketjap manis and toss until every grain is brown. Taste — it usually wants a little more ketjap or a pinch of salt.
Serve with a fried egg on top and cucumber on the side.
tips: Prawn crackers (kroepoek) are on the same shelf as the ketjap and take 20 seconds in hot oil.
For bami goreng, swap the rice for 200 g cooked egg noodles and keep everything else identical.

title: Chicken Teriyaki Rice Bowl
blurb: Four ingredients make real teriyaki sauce, and none of them is a bottle labelled teriyaki. Weeknight food that children eat without argument.
steps: Rice on first: rinse, 150 g rice to 190 ml water, lid on, 12 minutes low, then 10 minutes off the heat with the lid still on.
Mix the soy, mirin, sugar and ginger in a cup.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high. Lay the thighs in smooth side down and leave them for 5 minutes without touching — you want a proper brown crust.
Flip, cook 4 minutes more. Meanwhile steam or boil the broccoli for 3 minutes until bright green and still firm.
Pour the sauce into the pan. It will bubble hard and reduce; turn the chicken every 30 seconds for about 2 minutes until the sauce is syrupy and clinging.
Rest the chicken for 2 minutes, then slice across into thick strips.
Rice into bowls, chicken on top, spoon over every drop of pan sauce. Broccoli alongside, spring onion and sesame over the lot.
tips: No mirin: 4 tbsp dry sherry or white wine plus 2 extra tsp sugar. Non-alcoholic: 3 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tbsp water and 2 extra tsp sugar.
The sauce reduces fast at the end. If it goes past syrup to toffee, a tablespoon of water brings it back.

title: Thai Green Curry
blurb: The technique that separates good from bland: fry the paste in coconut cream until the oil splits out before anything else goes in.

ingredients.prep: bruised with the back of a knife

steps: Open the coconut milk without shaking it. Spoon the thick cream from the top into a cold pan — about 4 tablespoons.

Heat it until it bubbles and you see clear oil separating at the edges, 3-4 minutes. Add the curry paste and fry it hard for 2 minutes, stirring. This is the step everyone skips and it is the whole dish.
Chicken in, turning it in the paste for 3 minutes until coated and sealed.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk plus 100 ml water, add the lemongrass if you have it, and simmer 8 minutes.
Beans and pepper in for a final 5 minutes — they should keep some bite.
Off the heat, season with the fish sauce, sugar and the juice of half the lime. Taste and push it around: more fish sauce for salt, more sugar for roundness, more lime for lift.
Tear in the basil, serve with jasmine rice and the rest of the lime in wedges.
tips: European supermarket curry paste is milder than Thai. Three tablespoons is a starting point, not a limit.
Vegetarian version: swap chicken for 400 g firm tofu and fish sauce for 2 tbsp light soy plus an extra pinch of sugar. Check the paste — some contain shrimp.

title: Beef & Broccoli
blurb: Cheap frying steak turned tender by cornflour and thirty seconds of restraint. The sauce is five things you already own.

ingredients.prep: sliced 3 mm thick across the grain
small florets, stalk peeled and sliced

steps: Toss the beef with 2 tsp cornflour and 1 tbsp of the soy sauce. Leave 15 minutes while the rice cooks and you chop.
Boil the broccoli for 2 minutes, then drain it very well. Wet broccoli steams the beef instead of frying it.
Mix the sauce: remaining 2 tbsp soy, oyster sauce, sherry, sugar, the last 1 tsp cornflour and 4 tbsp water.

Wok or big pan as hot as it goes, 1 tbsp oil. Half the beef, spread out, 90 seconds without stirring, then 30 seconds tossing. Out onto a plate. Repeat with the second half — crowding the pan is the classic mistake.
Last tablespoon of oil, garlic and ginger, 20 seconds. Broccoli in, 1 minute.
Beef back in, sauce poured down the side of the pan. Toss for 45 seconds until it thickens and coats everything.
Sesame oil off the heat, straight onto rice.
tips: Slicing is easier if the beef goes in the freezer for 15 minutes first.
Vegetarian: use mushroom stir-fry sauce instead of oyster and 300 g pressed firm tofu.

title: Vegetable Pad Thai
blurb: Tamarind is the one thing you cannot buy at Lidl, so this uses the lime-and-brown-sugar route that Thai cooks abroad use anyway.
steps: Pour just-boiled water over the rice noodles in a bowl, off the heat. Leave 7 minutes until bendy but still firm in the middle, then drain and rinse cold. They finish cooking in the pan.
Whisk the sauce: brown sugar, soy, vinegar, sambal and the juice of the whole lime. It should taste aggressively sweet-sour-salty on its own.
Dry the tofu on kitchen paper, then fry in 2 tbsp oil over high heat, 6-8 minutes, turning only when each side has browned. Set aside.
Last tablespoon of oil, garlic and carrot, 1 minute. Push everything to one side, pour the egg into the empty half and scramble it in loose curds.
Noodles and sauce in. Toss with tongs for 2 minutes — it will look wet, then suddenly the noodles drink it up and turn glossy.
Tofu back in with the beansprouts and spring onion, 30 seconds only so the sprouts stay crunchy.
Onto plates, peanuts and coriander over the top, extra lime on the side.
tips: If your store has tamarind paste, use 2 tbsp in place of the vinegar and half the lime — that is the real thing.
Vegan: leave out the egg and add 100 g extra tofu.

title: Bibimbap-style Rice Bowl
blurb: Separate piles of vegetables on rice, a fried egg, and gochujang sauce stirred through at the table. Assembly, not cooking.
steps: Rice on. Meanwhile marinate the beef in 2 tbsp soy, 1 tsp sugar, half the garlic and 1 tsp sesame oil.
Make the sauce: gochujang, 1 tbsp water, 1 tsp sugar, the vinegar and 1 tsp sesame oil. Stir smooth and set aside.
Wilt the spinach in a dry hot pan for 1 minute, squeeze out the water, then dress with 1 tsp sesame oil, a pinch of salt and the rest of the garlic.
Fry the mushrooms in 1 tbsp oil until browned and squeaky, season with the last tablespoon of soy. Out. Same pan, carrots for 2 minutes so they soften but keep colour. Out.
Pan on high, remaining oil, beef in one layer for 2 minutes until caramelised at the edges.
Fry the eggs so the whites are set and the yolks runny.

Rice into two wide bowls. Arrange the spinach, mushrooms, carrot, cucumber and beef in separate piles on top, egg in the middle, sesame seeds over. Sauce on the side — everyone stirs their own bowl into a mess, which is the point.
tips: No gochujang: 1 tbsp sambal oelek, 1 tsp miso and 2 tsp honey gets close.
Works with anything in the fridge. Courgette, beansprouts and pointed cabbage are all traditional-adjacent.

title: Mapo Tofu
blurb: Silky tofu in a fierce red sauce. The authentic broad bean paste is a specialty-shop item, so this rebuilds it from sambal and miso.
steps: Slide the tofu cubes into a pan of salted simmering water and leave them off the heat while you cook. It firms them up and stops them breaking later.
Dissolve the stock cube in 250 ml hot water. Mix the cornflour with 2 tbsp cold water in a separate cup.
Oil in a wide pan on high. Pork mince in, pressed flat, and left to brown properly for 3 minutes before you break it up. Brown, not grey.
Heat down to medium. Sambal, miso, garlic and ginger, fried for 90 seconds until the oil turns red.
Pour in the stock and the soy. Drain the tofu and slide it in. Simmer 5 minutes, pushing the tofu gently with the back of a spoon rather than stirring.
Stir the cornflour slurry and add it in two goes, letting it bubble between, until the sauce coats a spoon.
Spring onion and the ground Sichuan pepper over the top. Serve on rice with something plain and green alongside.
tips: Vegetarian: leave out the pork and brown 150 g finely chopped mushrooms instead — same depth.
If you find doubanjiang (broad bean paste) in an Asian shop, use 2 tbsp of it in place of the sambal and miso and you have the real thing.

title: Chicken Satay with Peanut Sauce
blurb: Made entirely from things in a Dutch supermarket, and better than any jar. The sauce keeps a week and improves on day two.
steps: Marinate the chicken in 2 tbsp of the ketjap, half the garlic, the coriander, cumin, turmeric and 1 tbsp oil. Twenty minutes on the counter, or overnight in the fridge.
Sauce: gently heat the remaining garlic in 1 tbsp oil for 30 seconds, then stir in the peanut butter, coconut milk, the other 2 tbsp ketjap and the sambal.
Let it bubble for 3-4 minutes until it thickens and darkens, loosening with a splash of water if it seizes. Finish with the juice of half the lime. Taste: it wants to be salty-sweet with a low burn.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or don't — loose chunks cook just as well.
Grill under a hot oven grill for 12 minutes, turning halfway, until charred at the edges. A ridged pan or a barbecue is better still. The ketjap catches quickly, which is what you want.
Serve with rice, the warm peanut sauce poured over, cucumber on the side and the rest of the lime.
tips: Soak wooden skewers 20 minutes first, or they burn.
The sauce is also the dressing for gado-gado: pour it over boiled potatoes, green beans, beansprouts and a hard-boiled egg.

title: Weeknight Chicken Pho
blurb: Real pho broth takes six hours. This charred-onion shortcut takes twenty-five minutes and is honest about the difference.
steps: Put the onion halves and ginger cut-side down in a dry pan over high heat. Leave 5 minutes until properly blackened. This is where the smoky depth comes from, so let them go further than feels sensible.
Add 1.2 litres water, the stock cubes, star anise, cinnamon and ground coriander. Bring to a simmer.
Slide in the chicken thighs and poach at the barest simmer for 18 minutes. Do not let it boil or the broth goes cloudy.
Lift out the chicken and shred it with two forks. Strain the broth and season with the fish sauce and sugar. It should taste slightly too savoury on its own — the noodles absorb a lot.
Soak the rice noodles in just-boiled water for 6 minutes, drain.
Noodles into deep bowls, chicken on top, ladle over the hot broth.
Everything else goes on the table: beansprouts, herbs, lime, chilli, sriracha. Building the bowl is the diner's job, not the cook's.
tips: Toasting the star anise and cinnamon in the dry pan with the onion for the last minute is worth the ten seconds.
Beef version: use beef stock and lay paper-thin raw steak in the bowl — the boiling broth cooks it as you pour.

title: Bánh Mì
blurb: A European baguette is the whole reason this sandwich exists. The pickle needs twenty minutes, and everything else is assembly.
steps: Pickle first: dissolve the white sugar and 1/2 tsp salt in the vinegar plus 4 tbsp warm water. Add the carrot and radish and leave for at least 20 minutes, tossing once.
Fry the pork in the oil over high heat, pressed flat, until it is properly browned in patches — 5 minutes, resisting the urge to stir.
Add the garlic, then the fish sauce, soy and brown sugar. Cook 2 minutes more until sticky and glazed.
Split the baguette lengthways, keeping a hinge, and toast it cut side up for 2 minutes so it can hold a wet filling.
Spread sriracha along the bottom. Cucumber strips, then the hot pork, then a generous handful of drained pickle.
Coriander and chilli on top, press the lid down hard, cut in half.
tips: Mayonnaise on the top half is traditional and makes it far better.
The pickle keeps a fortnight in a jar in the fridge and improves everything it touches.

title: Red Curry Salmon
blurb: Twenty-five minutes start to finish. The salmon goes in last and poaches in the curry, so it never overcooks.
steps: Rice on first — it takes the longest.
Spoon the thick cream off the top of the coconut milk into a pan and heat until it splits and the oil shows, 3 minutes.
Curry paste in, fried for 2 minutes until dark and fragrant.
Rest of the coconut milk in, plus 50 ml water. Simmer 5 minutes to thicken slightly.
Pepper and sugar snaps in for 3 minutes, then lay the salmon chunks on top, lid on, and poach for 4 minutes without stirring. Nudge, don't stir, or the fish breaks up.
Off the heat, stir the spinach through until it wilts. Season with fish sauce, sugar and lime juice.
Coriander over, rice underneath.
tips: Cod, pollock or prawns all work — prawns need 2 minutes, not 4.
A tablespoon of peanut butter stirred into the sauce turns this into something closer to a massaman.

title: Egg Fried Rice
blurb: Fifteen minutes, five ingredients, and one rule: the rice must be cold. Everything else is negotiable.

ingredients.prep: beaten with a pinch of salt

steps: Get the pan properly hot before anything goes in. This dish is about heat, not time.
1 tbsp oil, pour in the egg, and let it set for 20 seconds before scrambling it into large soft curds. Tip it out while still slightly underdone.
Second tablespoon of oil. Carrot and sugar snaps if using, 2 minutes. Then garlic and spring onion whites, 30 seconds.
Cold rice in. Press it against the pan and let it sit for 30 seconds at a time between stirs — you are toasting the grains, not steaming them. Three minutes.
Egg back in, broken into pieces. Soy sauce poured around the edge of the pan so it sizzles rather than pools.
Sesame oil and the green spring onion tops off the heat. Serve immediately.
tips: No cold rice? Cook it, spread it thin on a tray and give it 20 minutes in the freezer.
Leftover roast chicken, frozen peas, or the last of a bag of prawns all belong here.

title: Singapore Noodles
blurb: Curry powder in a Chinese stir-fry — a colonial accident that became a classic. Ordinary European kerrie is exactly the right stuff.
steps: Soak the vermicelli in just-boiled water for 3 minutes only, then drain, rinse cold and cut through the nest a few times with scissors so it doesn't become one solid rope.
Mix the curry powder and turmeric with the soy, sherry, sugar and 3 tbsp water.
Hot pan, 1 tbsp oil, scramble the eggs into loose curds and set aside.
1 tbsp oil, prawns in a single layer for 90 seconds a side until just pink. Out — they will finish later.
Last tablespoon of oil, onion and pepper for 2 minutes, then garlic for 30 seconds.
Noodles in with the curry sauce. Toss constantly with tongs for 2 minutes until every strand is yellow. Add a splash of water if it looks dry — the noodles drink more than you expect.
Prawns, egg, beansprouts and spring onion back in for 45 seconds. Sesame oil off the heat.
tips: Char siu pork from this app, sliced thin, is the traditional partner to the prawns.
Vegetarian: skip the prawns, double the egg and add 150 g fried tofu.

title: Japanese Curry Rice
blurb: The boxed roux blocks are a specialty import. Making the roux yourself takes four minutes and costs almost nothing.
steps: Brown the chicken in the oil in a large pan, 5 minutes. Add the onions and cook 5 minutes more until they collapse and sweeten.
Carrot and potato in with 700 ml water and the stock cubes. Simmer 15 minutes until the potato is tender.
Meanwhile, the roux: melt the butter in a small pan, stir in the flour and cook over low heat for 3 minutes until it smells like biscuits and turns the colour of sand.
Off the heat, stir the curry powder and garam masala into the roux. It will look like wet sand.
Ladle three spoonfuls of the hot cooking liquid into the roux and whisk to a smooth paste, then scrape all of it back into the main pan.
Add the soy, honey and ketchup. Simmer 5 minutes, stirring, until it thickens to a thick gravy that holds a line on the back of a spoon.
Serve in a wide bowl, curry on one half, rice on the other.
tips: Grated apple is the classic secret ingredient — half an apple added with the onions.
Better the next day, and it freezes well. Make the full four portions even if you are two.

title: Chicken Katsu
blurb: Panko is the only thing that makes this work, and it is the one specialty item worth going out of your way for.

ingredients.prep: shredded as finely as you can

steps: Katsu sauce: stir the ketchup, soy, oyster sauce and honey together. That is the whole sauce, and it tastes remarkably like the bottled stuff.
Season the chicken well. Three shallow bowls: flour, egg, panko.
Flour the chicken and shake off the excess, then egg, then press hard into the panko on both sides. Press, don't dip — the crumbs need to embed.
Heat 1 cm of oil in a frying pan to about 175 °C. A panko crumb should sizzle briskly, not violently.
Fry 3-4 minutes a side until deep golden. Drain on a rack, not on paper, so the underside stays crisp.
Rest 2 minutes, then slice across into 2 cm strips.
Serve on rice with a mountain of raw shredded cabbage, a squeeze of lime over the cabbage, and the sauce poured over the chicken.
tips: The raw cabbage is not a garnish. It cuts the fried richness and is how it is eaten in Japan.
Pork loin steaks make tonkatsu with no other change. Aubergine slices work for a vegetarian version.

title: Oven Char Siu Pork
blurb: The sticky red pork from the takeaway window, done in a normal oven. Marinate in the morning, roast in the evening.
steps: Mix the hoisin, soy, 2 tbsp of the honey, sherry, five-spice, garlic, ginger and sugar. Keep 3 tablespoons of it back in a separate cup — that is your glaze, and it must not touch raw pork.
Coat the pork in the rest and refrigerate. Four hours minimum, overnight for real depth.
Oven to 200 °C. Sit the pork on a rack over a roasting tin with 1 cm of water in the bottom — the water stops the drips burning and smoking out your kitchen.
Roast 20 minutes. Turn, brush with the reserved glaze, roast 10 minutes more.

Stir the last tablespoon of honey into what remains of the glaze, brush it on, and give it a final 5 minutes until the edges are dark and lacquered. Watch it — the sugar goes from caramel to carbon quickly.
Rest 10 minutes before slicing across the grain. Meanwhile steam the pak choi for 3 minutes.
Serve sliced over rice with the greens and any juices from the board.
tips: The classic red colour comes from food colouring. It tastes the same without it.
Leftovers are the best possible addition to fried rice, Singapore noodles or a bowl of instant ramen.

title: Miso-Glazed Aubergine
blurb: Three tablespoons of glaze turn a cheap aubergine into the best thing on the table. Almost no work.

ingredients.prep: halved lengthways, flesh scored in a diamond pattern

steps: Oven to 200 °C. Brush the cut faces of the aubergine generously with the sunflower oil — aubergine drinks oil, and underdone aubergine is unpleasant, so be generous.
Roast cut side up for 20 minutes until the flesh is completely soft and collapsing when pressed.
Meanwhile whisk the miso, mirin, sugar and sesame oil into a thick, spreadable glaze.
Spread the glaze over the roasted faces, right into the scored cuts.
Back in under a hot grill for 3-5 minutes until the glaze bubbles and blackens in patches. Do not walk away — miso burns fast.
Sesame seeds and spring onion over the top. Serve with rice, one half each.
tips: No mirin: 2 tbsp rice vinegar plus an extra teaspoon of sugar.
The same glaze is excellent on salmon — grill it for 4 minutes.

title: Thai Basil Pork
blurb: Thailand's actual weeknight dinner. Twenty minutes, one pan, and a fried egg on top that is non-negotiable.
steps: Rice on. Mix the oyster sauce, soy, fish sauce and sugar in a cup.
Fry the eggs first, in 2 tbsp of oil over high heat, spooning hot oil over the tops until the whites are blistered and lacy and the yolk is still liquid. Set aside on kitchen paper.
Same pan, remaining oil, high heat. Garlic and chilli for 20 seconds only.
Pork in, pressed flat, left for 2 minutes to brown before you break it up. Then stir-fry 3 minutes more.
Green beans in for 2 minutes if using, then pour in the sauce and let it bubble and reduce for 1 minute.
Off the heat, throw in the basil and stir until it just wilts — 15 seconds. Any longer and it turns black.
Over rice with the fried egg on top. Break the yolk into the pork.
tips: Holy basil is what Thailand uses and no European supermarket has it. Italian basil plus an extra chilli and the fish sauce lands close enough that this is worth cooking anyway.
Chicken mince works identically. So does firm tofu, crumbled.

title: Sweet & Sour Chicken
blurb: Rescued from the neon-orange version. Real pineapple, real vinegar, and a sauce built on ketchup without apology.
steps: Toss the chicken with the egg, then with 4 tbsp of the cornflour and a good pinch of salt, until each piece wears a dry, craggy coat.
Sauce: 150 ml of the reserved pineapple juice, the ketchup, vinegar, sugar, soy and the last tablespoon of cornflour, whisked smooth.
Heat 1 cm of oil in a frying pan. Fry the chicken in two batches, 4 minutes a batch, until golden and crisp. Drain on a rack.
Pour off all but a tablespoon of the oil. Onion and pepper on high heat for 2 minutes — they should stay crunchy.
Garlic for 20 seconds, then the pineapple chunks for 1 minute.
Stir the sauce again and pour it in. It thickens and turns glossy within a minute.
Chicken back in, tossed for 20 seconds only so it stays crisp. Straight to the table over rice.
tips: Frying the chicken twice — once at 4 minutes, cooled, then 90 seconds more just before serving — makes it stay crisp under the sauce.
Pork shoulder in the same batter is the Cantonese original.

title: Weeknight Miso Ramen
blurb: Instant noodle blocks, a broth you build in fifteen minutes, and a jammy egg. Nothing like a twelve-hour tonkotsu, and still very good.
steps: Eggs first: 6.5 minutes in boiling water, then straight into cold water. Peel when cool — the yolk should be soft, not runny, not set.
Brown the pork mince hard in the sunflower oil, 5 minutes, until there are genuinely crisp brown bits. Add half the garlic and ginger for the last minute. Scoop out and keep warm.
Same pan, 1 litre water and the stock cubes. Simmer with the remaining garlic and ginger for 10 minutes.
Take a ladle of the hot broth and whisk the miso into it in a separate bowl, then pour it back. Never boil miso in the pot — it goes grainy and loses its edge.
Season with the soy and sesame oil. Taste; it should be noticeably savoury.
Boil the noodle blocks for 2 minutes in a separate pan of water (not the broth — the starch cloudies it). Blanch the pak choi in the same water for the last minute.
Noodles into deep bowls, broth over, then arrange pork, pak choi, halved egg, spring onion and nori on top. Sweet chilli drizzled over if you like heat.
tips: Char siu from this app, sliced thin, replaces the mince and turns this into something close to the real thing.
Vegetarian: vegetable stock, 200 g fried mushrooms in place of the pork, and check your miso.

title: Red Lentil Dal with Tadka
blurb: Costs under three euros and every single ingredient is in the cheapest aisle. The tadka poured over at the end is the entire point.
steps: Put the lentils in a pan with 900 ml water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer 20 minutes until they collapse into a loose porridge. Stir now and then so the bottom doesn't catch.
While it cooks, fry the onion in 1 tbsp of the oil for 8 minutes until properly golden — not pale, golden.
Add half the garlic, the ginger, cumin and ground coriander. One minute, then the tomatoes, and cook 5 minutes until they break down into a thick paste.
Stir this into the lentils with the garam masala. Loosen with hot water until it pours slowly off a spoon. Taste for salt — dal needs more than you think.
The tadka: heat the remaining 3 tbsp oil in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the rest of the sliced garlic and fry until it turns pale gold, about 40 seconds, then the chilli flakes for 5 seconds.
Pour the whole sizzling lot over the dal in the pot. It will hiss dramatically. Stir it through only half way, so there are streaks.
Lime juice and fresh coriander. Serve with basmati.
tips: Take the garlic off the heat while it is pale gold — it keeps darkening in the hot oil and burnt garlic ruins the pot.
A spoon of the tadka oil over plain rice the next day is one of the great cheap lunches.

title: Weeknight Butter Chicken
blurb: No tandoor, no cream by the litre, no three-hour marinade. Yoghurt does the tenderising and the sauce comes together in one pan.
steps: Marinate the chicken in the yoghurt, 2 tsp garam masala, the turmeric, cumin, paprika, half the garlic and half the ginger. Fifteen minutes is enough; two hours is better.
Spread it on a foil-lined tray and grill on the highest oven setting for 12 minutes, turning once, until charred at the edges. Those black bits are standing in for the tandoor, so let them happen.
Meanwhile melt half the butter in a wide pan. Remaining garlic and ginger for 1 minute, then the tomato purée for another minute until it darkens.
Tinned tomatoes in, plus 100 ml water and the sugar. Simmer 12 minutes, then blend smooth with a stick blender. This is what makes it taste like a restaurant instead of a stew.
Stir in the cream, the last teaspoon of garam masala and the rest of the butter in small pieces, off the heat, so it emulsifies rather than splits.
Chicken in along with every drop of juice from the tray. Simmer 5 minutes.
Salt to taste, coriander over, basmati alongside.
tips: Kasoori methi (dried fenugreek leaf) is the flavour you cannot place in restaurant versions. If you ever see it, crush a teaspoon in at the end.
Coconut milk instead of cream makes it dairy-free apart from the butter, which you can swap for oil.

title: Bami Goreng
blurb: Nasi goreng's noodle sibling and the Dutch takeaway standard. One pan, twenty-five minutes, no specialty shopping.
steps: Boil the egg noodles 1 minute less than the packet says. Drain, rinse cold, toss with a teaspoon of oil so they don't fuse.
Hot pan, 1 tbsp oil. Pour in the beaten egg, let it set into a thin omelette, then slide it out and cut into ribbons.
Remaining oil, high heat. Chicken for 4 minutes until browned. Onion and carrot for 3 minutes more.
Garlic, sambal and ground coriander, 30 seconds. Then the cabbage, 2 minutes — it should keep some crunch.
Noodles in with the ketjap and soy. Toss with tongs until every strand is uniformly brown, about 2 minutes, letting it catch on the pan between tosses.
Beansprouts, spring onion and egg ribbons folded through for the last 30 seconds.
Straight onto plates. Extra sambal on the side.
tips: Fried onions (gebakken uitjes) from a tub scattered over the top is exactly how it is served in the Netherlands.
Leftover roast chicken or ham works instead of raw chicken — add it with the noodles.

title: Gochujang Chicken Traybake
blurb: Everything on one tray, into the oven, done. The glaze caramelises against the potatoes and there is nothing to wash up.
steps: Oven to 200 °C. Whisk the gochujang, soy, honey, vinegar, sesame oil, garlic and ginger into a glaze.
Toss the potatoes and onion wedges with the sunflower oil and a good pinch of salt, and spread them over a large roasting tray. Give them a 15-minute head start in the oven.
Coat the chicken thighs in two thirds of the glaze.
Push the potatoes aside and lay the chicken among them, skin or smooth side up. Roast 25 minutes.
Brush with the remaining glaze and give it 8 more minutes, until the edges are dark and sticky and the potatoes have soaked up the run-off.
Rest 5 minutes, then scatter with spring onion and sesame seeds. Rice on the side to mop the tray.
tips: Kimchi on the side, straight from the jar, cuts the sweetness perfectly.
No gochujang: 2 tbsp sambal oelek, 1 tbsp miso and an extra tablespoon of honey.
